chapter: Hite tours, postwar L.A. and the Central Avenue scene
title: Why San Diego never had a jazz scene
summary: San Diego was a sailor town with the Creole Palace as chorus-line nightclub.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: Speaking of San Diego, where you wouldn't hardly go at that time, did you make enough trips to
San Diego to know much about the jazz scene down there, because there's very little that seems to be known about it (inaudible).

There was very, very little jazz scene ever in San Diego for the simple reason that that was a sailor town and when we say a sailor town, we just mean a sailor town. Sailors in the old days had a certain type of things that they liked and it wasn't high-class jazz. They liked to be nostalgic and have some guy sing "Harbor Lights" to them or, you know, all of those kind of things, to remind them of when they were away on their ship, wondering what their girl was doing back on the seashore, you know? It was a sailor town.
I know there were a couple of jazz clubs down in the 40s and before that, nothing? I've heard that there was a place called the Creole Palace.

Nope, the Creole Palace was not a jazz joint. The Creole Palace was a hotel and it had a nightclub downstairs that had chorus girls in it and an orchestra and that's what it was. It was not a jazz place.

As jazz goes, jazz hardly never got to San Diego. The Creole Palace was a nightclub on the order of the Club Alabam, all black, with six or eight chorus girls in the line, comedians and a singer and a couple of tapdancers and that was it.
